newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland honours rival symbols of conflict.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland honours rival symbols of conflict.

text.p: Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, said on Sunday's anniversary of the IRA bomb that killed two people and derailed peace that it was time Protestants stopped demonising his Catholic supporters.
Hours earlier, hundreds of Protestants chanting abuse marched angrily past a Catholic church demanding that Catholics should stop demonising the pro-British majority.

The twin ceremonies illustrated the gulf of distrust that has widened since the Irish Republican Army renewed its war against British rule by ending a 17-month truce with a bomb at London's Canary Wharf complex.

Polarised since Northern Ireland was established seven decades ago, the two communities have retreated behind mental and physical barricades since the breakdown of an August 1994 IRA ceasefire which ushered in a short-lived honeymoon of peace.

Spokesmen for mainstream political parties attend weekly peace talks but say they are going nowhere fast while the two communities live separate lives and honour different flags - Protestants Britain's Union Jack, Catholics the Irish tricolour.
Adams made his remarks at a brief Belfast ceremony to honour seven taxi drivers killed by Protestant Loyalist gunmen to avenge IRA attacks between 1975 and 1972.

He spoke at the West Belfast taxi rank that Catholics have used to ferry them from Catholic enclaves to the shopping centre since Northern Ireland erupted into sectarian violence at the start of the 27-year "Troubles".
A few minutes' walk away, a similar taxi rank using identical black London taxis exists to serve the needs of the 60 percent Protestant majority, which wants to say British.

Adams and families of the dead attended a brief city-centre mass and then walked to the unveiling of a black stone monument surrounded by Celtic heraldry which listed the names of the victims "murdered in the service of the community."

The Sinn Fein leader, barred from faltering Belfast peace talks until the IRA calls a permanent truce, said :"The reason these men were killed is because of a policy of demonisation of an entire community, a policy of treating it as a terrorist community, a community referred to as barbaric."
Symbols abounded. A priest conducted a brief service in Irish, a language militant Catholics say was suppressed by British settlers to stifle their true identity.

Adams spoke in Irish for the families and English for the television crews; around him, signs in English and Irish denoted where passengers should queue for taxis to their suburbs. Belfast in English is Bheal Feirste in Irish.
Overhead, a military spy-in-the-sky army helicopter hovered over Protestant and Catholic suburbs as it has every day since the IRA truce ended at Canary Wharf.

In their respective suburbs, heraldic paintings on the gable ends of houses lionise the gunmen who claim to be defenders of their respective faiths, the IRA for Catholics and Ulster Freedom Fighters or Ulster Volunteer Force for Protestants.
Security sources say neither guerrilla army has more than a couple of hundred trigger-pulling militants, but their war has held the entire province hostage for a quarter of a century.

The IRA's Protestant counterparts are still officially abiding by a two-year-old truce but on Saturday night their backlash at Catholic militancy showed in an angry march in the suburb of Harryville in the town of Ballymena.

About one thousand Protestant Loyalists paraded British Union Jack flags and marched behind militaristic pipe bands in the 23rd week of protest against Catholic refusal to allow a Protestant parade at the nearby village of Dunloy.

The march was delayed by 30 minutes to allow Catholics attending a mass at the church to leave. But as the congregation prayed, Protestants coralled by police outside hurled abuse at "Fenians", a 19th-century Irish Republican brotherhood.

The chorus of one song, "We're up to here in Fenian blood," was audible inside the church. Later, Protestant youths pushed reporters off the street to clear the path for marchers carrying signs saying "Ulster Protestants demand parity of esteem."
As they walked past the church, masked youths taunted Royal Ulster Constabulary police guarding the church entrance as "Nazi bastards," "S.S. RUC" and "Fenian lovers."
